source.title: Sockpuppetting: Jailbreaking LLMs Without Optimization Through Output Prefix Injection

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The title in the supplied metadata differs slightly from the title in the paper text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests output-prefix injection and harmful-compliance rates on new instruction-tuned models, using prefill attacks and attack-success rate as the intervention and measure relevant to V4.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own prefill and optimized-suffix attack results. It does not test fine-tuning, benign data, per-token KL, decoding changes, parameter localization, or a training method for deepening safety. Claims and results it cites from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Reports prefill and optimized-suffix attack success rates on undefended instruction-tuned models, which bear on V4 (getting past the opening bypasses refusal). It is a different method from the original sources, which use fine-tuning and prefilling.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors conclude that cheap prefill ensembles reach high ASR on Llama and Qwen, and that rolling sockpuppetting beats their universal GCG baseline. They also state that part of that gain comes from the choice of target and that defences against output-prefix injection are needed. The record should add that the authors treat the prefill ensemble, not the optimized attack, as the more pressing threat.
record.recipe_differences: This paper evaluates output-prefix jailbreaks and gradient-optimized suffix placement, not fine-tuning. Its attack-success-rate experiments are relevant to the compliant-prefill part of V4 but use a different intervention from the original fine-tuning claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies by model, prefill wording/format, attack variant, and acceptance-sequence design. The authors report that equalizing the acceptance target substantially shrinks the placement advantage.
record.peer_reviewed: Published at the Second Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond (AIWILD) at ICML 2026
record.problems: Attack evaluations use a single greedy run per model and prompt. The authors note that small ASR differences may reflect run-to-run variation, that GCG uses a reimplementation with different hyperparameters and early stopping, and that absolute ASRs rely on a single lightly validated Gemma-3-27B-it judge. Some results are available only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted. The full set of individual values in Figures 2 and 3 is not transcribed where the figure text extraction does not give an unambiguous model-to-value assignment.

untested.parts: No per-token KL measurement between aligned and base models.
No parameter or rank localization experiment.
Only speculates about self-consistency; does not test whether data or objective produces shallow safety.
No deepening training intervention. Defences are mentioned only as future work.
Decoding changes are not tested. Only the three models, AdvBench and one judge were used.

missing.what: Prompt-only baseline ASRs per model (about 4-6% Gemma, 6% Llama, 0% Qwen read from Figure 2), GCG per-prompt rates, and the 520-prompt AdvBench results
Universal GCG baseline rates and the full-AdvBench (495-prompt) universal results, which the study says match the 100-prompt results closely
The ensemble on Llama drops from 90% on 100 prompts to 87.7% on the full 520-prompt AdvBench; the other two models agree closely

record.verdict_notes: The record's tranche T1 is wrong: the method is not the original fine-tuning method, so T2 fits better. R1 is a control and not an attack result. Results rest on a single greedy run and a single Gemma-3-27B judge that was only lightly validated. The paper does not apply the study's results to safety depth or the first-token view of shallow alignment.

versions.untested_parts: Tests compliant output prefills and optimized suffix attacks; does not test decoding changes or all possible suffixes and prefilled openings.
No parameter or rank localization experiment.
Discusses possible self-consistency and acceptance-sequence explanations, but does not test whether training data or objectives produce shallow safety.
No safety-deepening training intervention or test of whether it holds up.

rows.subject: Gemma-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen3-8B (all tested models, aggregate as reported)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated harmful prompts without an attack.
rows.value: over 93% refusal rate across all models
rows.note: Aggregate statement for the three models; individual prompt-only rates are shown in Figure 2.
rows.check: This is the no-attack control, not an attack result. An aggregate refusal rate of over 93% cannot show V4's bypass effect. It should be a baseline or control, not a verdict row.

rows.subject: Gemma-7B
rows.operation_detail: Ensembled PrefillAcceptance, PrefillNewline, and PrefillTitle; a prompt counts as successful if any variant elicits compliance.
rows.baseline: Prompt-only; exact individual rate not stated in text
rows.note: The ensemble raises compliance, but the reported rate is substantially lower than for Llama and Qwen.
rows.check: The 22% ensemble rate is correct, but the baseline is missing. Figure 2 shows the prompt-only rate for Gemma as about 4-6%, so the effect is clear but small, and the study itself calls Gemma more resistant to prefills.
